slides.0.title: Styles, sweetness and the label
slides.0.subtitle: NV, Vintage, Blanc de Blancs and reading the label
slides.1.title: The main Champagne styles
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Non-Vintage (NV)
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Blended across years as the house calling card, and the great majority of output (commonly estimated at 70–80%; sources differ, so not tested)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Vintage (Millésimé)
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Made from a single year, usually declared only in good years, with longer ageing (at least 36 months from bottling)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Blanc de Blancs / Blanc de Noirs
slides.1.highlights.2.content: The first uses only white grapes (Chardonnay), the second only black grapes (Pinot Noir, Meunier); both are white wines
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Rosé and Prestige Cuvée
slides.1.highlights.3.content: Champagne allows a little still red wine in the blend to make rosé (commonly about 5–20%) as well as skin contact; Prestige Cuvée is a house's flagship, not a legal category
slides.1.content: Level 2 covers the two rosé methods and prestige examples in more depth.
slides.2.title: Sweetness levels (dosage)
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Brut Nature / Extra Brut
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Brut Nature (Pas Dosé) 0–3 g/L with no added sugar; Extra Brut 0–6 g/L
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Brut (the most common)
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Under 12 g/L; Extra Dry is 12–17 g/L (sweeter than Brut, a misleading name)
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Sec / Demi-Sec / Doux
slides.2.highlights.3.title: A ±3 g/L tolerance
slides.2.highlights.3.content: The rules allow ±3 g/L on each category, so neighbouring bands overlap. We test the dry-to-sweet order, not the boundary values
slides.2.content: Dry to sweet: Brut Nature → Extra Brut → Brut → Extra Dry → Sec → Demi-Sec → Doux.
slides.3.title: Producer codes on the label
slides.3.highlights.0.title: NM: Négociant-Manipulant
slides.3.highlights.0.content: A house (most Grandes Marques), buying grapes or base wine and selling under its own brand
slides.3.highlights.1.title: RM: Récoltant-Manipulant
slides.3.highlights.1.content: A grower-producer making and selling Champagne from its own vineyards (Grower Champagne)
slides.3.highlights.2.title: CM / RC / SR
slides.3.highlights.2.content: CM: a cooperative brand; RC: a member selling cooperative-made wine; SR: a union of growers
slides.3.highlights.3.title: ND / MA
slides.3.highlights.3.content: ND: a distributor's brand; MA: a buyer's own brand (such as a supermarket or restaurant). The code is letters plus a registration number (such as RM-xxx-xxx), printed in small type at the foot of the label
slides.3.content: The code only tells you who made and sold the wine, not quality; the full labelling rules are in Level 3.
slides.4.title: How to read a label
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Required information
slides.4.highlights.0.content: The name "Champagne", sweetness term, alcohol, volume, producer code and name and country of origin; Brut is the most common sweetness term
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Minimum ageing
slides.4.highlights.1.content: NV needs at least 15 months from bottling (at least 12 on the lees) and Vintage at least 36 months; Loire Crémant has shorter rules, compare with the Loire course
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Disgorgement date (optional)
slides.4.highlights.2.content: Many producers voluntarily show the disgorgement date; time since disgorgement affects flavour development, covered in Level 2
slides.4.highlights.3.title: A reading order
slides.4.highlights.3.content: First the producer code (who made it), then sweetness (style), then vintage or NV (ageing), and finally style words such as Blanc de Blancs or Rosé
slides.4.content: The Level 3 lesson on regulation and label reading expands this into a full decoding routine.
slides.5.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
Which sweetness order, from driest to sweetest, is correct?
A. Brut → Extra Brut → Doux → Sec
B. Demi-Sec → Sec → Brut → Brut Nature
C. Extra Brut → Brut → Sec → Demi-Sec
D. Sec → Brut → Extra Brut → Doux
The right order is Brut Nature → Extra Brut → Brut → Extra Dry → Sec → Demi-Sec → Doux.
What does the label code RM stand for?
A. A grower making and selling wine from its own grapes
RM is Récoltant-Manipulant; houses are NM, cooperatives CM and buyers' brands MA.
What is the minimum ageing for Vintage Champagne?
A. At least 12 months from bottling
B. At least 15 months from bottling
D. At least 36 months from bottling
NV needs at least 15 months and Vintage at least 36 (three years).
